name: Siemens FirstSurge Pro FS140 Surge Device
summary: The best all-round choice for most homes, with the headroom to last through years of surges.
verdict: Siemens' FS140 is a high-capacity surge protective device rated by Siemens at 140 kA, listed for Type 1 or Type 2 installation. That flexibility lets an electrician mount it at the meter on the line side or, more commonly, wire it to a double-pole breaker in the panel. The enclosure is rated for indoor and outdoor use, and it is not tied to Siemens panels, so it works with any brand when wired to a breaker. Status LEDs show whether each protection mode is active, and the spec sheet lists protection across all modes for a split-phase service. Check the current spec sheet for its exact voltage protection rating and any surge counter or alarm features, as versions have varied. The housing is bigger than compact units, which can matter on cramped panels, and it costs more than basic devices, typically roughly $120 to $250 at the time of writing. For most homes, the extra capacity means a longer service life and more margin against larger external events.

name: Eaton CHSPT2ULTRA Ultra Surge Protective Device
summary: A high-capacity Type 2 device at a moderate price, and a common electrician favorite.
verdict: Eaton's CHSPT2ULTRA is a Type 2 surge protective device rated by Eaton at 108 kA, mounted through a panel knockout and wired to a double-pole breaker. It suits most residential load-center installs regardless of brand. Indicator LEDs show the status of each protection mode, and Eaton lists protection across each hot leg to neutral and to ground, plus neutral to ground. Electricians commonly use it as a default whole-house device because its capacity is high for the price, typically roughly $90 to $160 at the time of writing. Eaton also offers a connected-equipment warranty, but read the terms; claims typically depend on proper installation and grounding. The limitation is that it is Type 2 only, so it cannot be installed ahead of the main breaker. For most homes that is not an issue, since load-side installation is the norm. If you want one device that offers strong capacity without paying for the premium tier, this is the one to ask your electrician about.

name: Square D Home Electronics Protective Device HEPD80
summary: A compact, well-known device that suits most panels at a reasonable price.
verdict: Square D's HEPD80 is a compact surge protective device rated at 80 kA by Square D, designed for residential split-phase services. It mounts through a panel knockout or onto a nearby surface and wires to a double-pole breaker, so it fits nearly any panel, not just Square D's own. The small housing helps where space around the panel is tight, and LED indicators show the protection status. The 80 kA rating is plenty for most homes, though it gives less long-term headroom than 108 kA or 140 kA devices in areas with frequent lightning. Owners and electricians commonly mention that the indicator lights are small and can be hard to see, so mount it where you will check them. Price is typically roughly $70 to $130 at the time of writing. If you want a reputable device without paying for the highest capacity, the HEPD80 is a sound choice.

name: Intermatic IG2240-IMSK Surge Protective Device
summary: The right pick when the device needs to live outside next to the meter or service disconnect.
verdict: Intermatic's IG2240-IMSK is a surge protective device listed for Type 1 or Type 2 installation in a weather-resistant enclosure. That makes it a natural choice where the service disconnect is outdoors, which is common in warmer regions and newer homes where the main breaker sits next to the meter. Status indicators show whether protection is active. Intermatic has a long history in outdoor electrical equipment, and the IMSK suffix refers to a mounting kit for flexible installs. Its surge capacity is in the mid-range rather than the top tier, so check the current spec sheet for the exact kA and voltage protection ratings. Installation at or near the meter may require utility approval, and any line-side work must be done by a licensed electrician. Prices are typically roughly $80 to $160 at the time of writing. If your panel is indoors with room for a knockout, the Siemens or Eaton devices offer more capacity for similar money.

name: Leviton Panel Protector, Model 51120-1
summary: A solid, widely stocked device from a major brand, best for typical homes with modest surge exposure.
verdict: Leviton's 51120-1 is a Type 2 panel protector designed for 120/240-volt single-phase residential services. It mounts through a panel knockout and connects to a double-pole breaker, and it works with any panel brand. LED indicators show whether each protection mode is working. Leviton is a major wiring device maker, and the 51120-1 is stocked widely, which helps when you need one quickly. It also pairs with Leviton's range of receptacle-style and plug-in surge protectors for a layered system. Its capacity sits below premium devices, so it suits typical suburban homes with modest lightning exposure more than rural homes on long overhead lines. Leviton has released several versions over the years, so check the current spec sheet for the exact kA and voltage protection ratings. Price is typically roughly $90 to $170 at the time of writing. It is a reasonable choice if you prefer the Leviton ecosystem or find it readily at your supplier.

name: THQLSURGE Plug-In Surge Breaker from GE
summary: The simplest option for homes with a compatible GE panel and spare breaker spaces.
verdict: GE's THQLSURGE packages a surge protector in the shape of a double-pole breaker that plugs into two spaces in compatible GE load centers. There is no knockout, no external housing and no long leads, and the short connection to the bus is good for limiting let-through voltage. A pigtail connects to the neutral bar. For an electrician, it is one of the fastest installs available, and it typically costs roughly $70 to $130 at the time of writing. The constraints are significant. It fits only compatible GE panels, it needs two free breaker spaces, and its surge capacity is lower than external devices like the Siemens FS140 or Eaton CHSPT2ULTRA. Status indication is limited to a small indicator, so check it periodically. Other panel makers sell similar breaker-style devices for their own panels, such as Square D's QO and Homeline versions. If you have a compatible GE panel with room, it is the easiest way to add code-compliant surge protection.
